strengths: The paper presents a simple, moderately original architectural idea: dedicated input-derived anchor projections decouple cross-layer reuse from the first computational layer. Extending normalized mixing jointly to Q, K, V, and gate logits is a useful unification of value residuals and gated attention.

The experimental suite includes relevant parameter-scale baselines, internal- versus external-anchor variants, coefficient granularities, normalization ablations, and analyses of attention sinks, token similarity, intrinsic dimensionality, and learned mixing coefficients.

At the reported 450M scale, Dynamic ExoFormer improves over the base Transformer by 2.13 average-accuracy points and reduces perplexity from 14.79 to 14.09. It also outperforms the gated-attention and ResFormer baselines, suggesting potential practical value.

The architecture and training setup are generally presented clearly, and the appendix supplies major model and optimization hyperparameters. The figures reveal interesting qualitative structure, including approximately head-aligned value-mixing coefficients.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges the single model scale, restricted training budget, incomplete initialization search, multiple-choice-focused evaluation, and absence of formal theory. No immediate material ethical hazard is introduced by the method.
weaknesses: The principal evidence comes from one training run per configuration, with no seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. This is especially problematic because the direct static external-versus-internal-anchor differences are only 0.02 perplexity and 0.17 average-accuracy points for the elementwise variants, with external anchors sometimes reducing downstream accuracy at other granularities.

The strongest result uses dynamic mixing, but no Dynamic NuResFormer control is reported. Consequently, the experiment cannot determine how much of Dynamic ExoFormer's advantage comes from exogenous anchors rather than dynamic coefficients. A parameter-matched control for the four additional anchor projections is also absent.

The paper overstates its mechanistic conclusions. Token similarity, PCA dimensionality, and hidden-state trajectories do not establish that anchors preserve token identity or that sequential layers specialize in computation. The proposed Offloading Hypothesis needs causal interventions such as anchor removal or corruption by depth, token-identity probes, and comparisons against alternative persistent input pathways.

Several analysis metrics are insufficiently specified: the corpus and sample sizes, treatment of special or padding tokens, definition and aggregation of the attention-sink score, and the threshold/procedure producing “PCA core features” are not given. Figure 2 has no uncertainty estimates, so the representation claims are difficult to reproduce or assess statistically.

The abstract's claim of matching baseline loss with 1.84x fewer tokens is not accompanied by a tabulated measurement, uncertainty, or a clearly specified interpolation/crossing protocol. Likewise, the claimed 2x sink reduction applies to static ExoFormer relative to gated attention, while the dynamic model shows a smaller reduction.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the stated code/model release: the manuscript does not identify random seeds, tokenizer construction, exact FineWeb-Edu subset sampling, validation-set construction, evaluation harness/version, prompt templates, checkpoint-selection procedure, or sufficient implementation details for the dynamic per-token coefficients. There are also presentation inconsistencies such as references to nonexistent attention Stages 4 and 5.

The evaluation is confined to one 450M regime and six closely related multiple-choice benchmarks. There are no generation, long-context, robustness, throughput, memory, or larger-scale experiments, limiting the demonstrated significance and generality. The paper honestly notes part of this limitation, but the central claims are still phrased broadly.

Research-ethics treatment is minimal: although risks are low for an architectural paper, the manuscript does not discuss biases, privacy, or licensing considerations associated with web-crawled FineWeb-Edu data, nor the compute and environmental cost of the experiment suite.

strengths: The normalized Q/K/V/gate mixing framework and dedicated input-derived anchor are simple, intelligible architectural ideas that extend value residual learning in a potentially useful direction.

The experiments include relevant baselines, roughly parameter-matched models, three coefficient granularities, pathway/normalization ablations, training curves, and representation analyses. The main training hyperparameters are also reported. Dynamic ExoFormer obtains the best reported perplexity (14.09 versus 14.79 for the base Transformer and 14.15 for NuResFormer) and the best mean benchmark accuracy (50.27% versus 48.14% and 49.68%, respectively). These results suggest that the mechanism merits further study.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges the modest 454M-scale experiment, lack of an exhaustive initialization search, narrow multiple-choice evaluation, and absence of formal theory.
weaknesses: Soundness: all results appear to come from one training run per configuration, with no seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The decisive downstream gain over the strongest relevant static baselines is only about 0.6 points, and individual tasks are mixed. With many variants evaluated and the best one highlighted, neither this gain nor the very small 14.15-to-14.09 perplexity difference is convincingly distinguishable from training or evaluation variance.

The central first-layer-tension and Offloading Hypothesis claims are not established by the evidence. Token cosine similarity, PCA dimensionality, gate activation, and input similarity are observational correlates and do not demonstrate that anchors preserve token identity or that layers specialize in computation/refinement. No causal intervention, anchor removal at inference, information-recovery probe, controlled anchor-capacity experiment, or direct measurement of identity preservation is provided. Statements that the evidence “confirms” the proposed mechanism therefore substantially overreach.

The comparison does not isolate several causal factors. ExoFormer adds four projection matrices and approximately 4M parameters without an equal-capacity control; the dynamic variant lacks a dynamic NuResFormer/internal-anchor control; and gated models use 29 layers while the ungated baseline uses 32. Thus the headline 2.13-point improvement over the base Transformer conflates external anchors, gating, dynamic mixing, parameter allocation, and depth.

The claimed 1.84x token efficiency is inferred from a single training curve without uncertainty, a precise matching protocol, or compute-normalized accounting. ExoFormer performs additional projections and has more parameters, so equal-token comparisons alone do not establish training-compute efficiency. Runtime, FLOPs, memory, and wall-clock measurements are absent.

The representation study is insufficiently specified for reproduction: the manuscript does not clearly define the sample corpus and size, head/token/layer aggregation, attention-sink statistic, entropy normalization, or the variance threshold used for “PCA core features.” Table 2 averages quantities whose averaging procedure is unclear. The interpretation of a local cosine-similarity minimum as the start of a refinement phase is especially speculative.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter disclosure. The exact FineWeb-Edu subset and ordering, tokenizer details, random seeds, evaluation harness and prompt templates, checkpoint-selection rule, and run-to-run variability are missing. The text promises released code and models, but the supplied manuscript contains no usable repository or artifact link.

Significance and originality are presently moderate rather than compelling. The method mainly combines and extends known value residuals, gating, normalization, and context-conditioned mixing. Evidence is limited to one 454M model family, 10B training tokens, a 2048-token context, and six conventional multiple-choice benchmarks; there is no generation, long-context, scaling, or transfer evaluation.

Presentation is generally readable, but several figures have very small labels, important analysis definitions are absent, and some captions are inaccurate—for example, Table 1 says it reports validation loss although it reports perplexity. The prose repeatedly elevates hypotheses into causal conclusions.

The paper has no dedicated ethics discussion. This is not an acute ethical blocker for an architectural study, but it should address the provenance and possible biases of web-crawled FineWeb-Edu data, benchmark contamination, released-model risks, and computational cost. The limitations section also omits the most consequential evidential limitations: single-run results and the non-causal nature of the mechanistic account.

Originality: Mixing normalized anchor projections across Q, K, V, and gate logits provides a useful generalization of value residual learning. Moving the anchor outside the sequential stack is simple, conceptually clean, and appears novel relative to the cited residual-mixing methods.

Significance: The combination of improved perplexity, a 2.13-point average accuracy gain over the base model, and substantially reduced attention sinks is promising. The method adds little parameter overhead and could be practically useful if the gains persist at larger scales.

The ablation coverage is unusually helpful: the paper compares internal and external anchors, normalized and unnormalized variants, three coefficient granularities, dynamic mixing, gated attention, value residuals, and their naïve combination.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture and initialization are described with explicit equations, and the appendix reports model dimensions, optimizer settings, learning rates, training steps, and detailed per-task results. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges the modest scale, restricted task coverage, and absence of formal theory.

The representation analyses reveal an interesting empirical phenomenon: external anchors improve task metrics despite higher token similarity and lower estimated intrinsic dimensionality. Even if the proposed explanation is not yet established, this is a worthwhile observation for subsequent work.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that separating the anchor role from computation explains the improvement—is not decisively established. The closest static comparison is very small: E-ExoFormer versus E-NuResFormer changes perplexity from 14.15 to 14.13 and average accuracy from 49.68% to 49.85%. There is no dynamic internal-anchor control corresponding to Dynamic ExoFormer, so the best result conflates dynamic mixing with anchor decoupling.

All reported results appear to be single runs, with no random-seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly consequential for the noisy multiple-choice accuracies and the small differences among ExoFormer, NuResFormer, and ResFormer variants.

The offloading hypothesis is substantially stronger than its evidence. Token-to-token cosine similarity, PCA feature counts, and similarity to input embeddings do not directly demonstrate that anchors preserve token identity or that sequential layers specialize in computation. No intervention, anchor ablation at inference, information-probing experiment, or causal mediation test supports that interpretation.

Several representation-analysis details needed to assess the claims are missing: the PCA variance threshold, sampled data and token positions, aggregation procedure, attention-sink definition, and uncertainty across examples. Calling the observed geometry “representation collapse” may also be misleading because the model retains strong predictive performance and receives anchor information at every layer.

The 1.84× data-efficiency claim is inferred from a single training-curve crossing without a precise matching protocol or uncertainty. Likewise, the comparison with the 32-layer base Transformer is complicated by gated models having 29 layers and ExoFormer having approximately four million additional parameters; FLOPs, throughput, and memory costs are not reported.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful hyperparameter table. The manuscript does not specify random seeds, tokenizer identity, exact FineWeb-Edu subset construction, data order, evaluation harness/version, prompt templates, or all definitions used for diagnostic metrics. It promises released code and models, but no usable anonymized artifact is evident in the manuscript.

Presentation is generally clear, but some figures have very small axes and legends, and several mechanistic conclusions are phrased too definitively relative to correlational plots. The statement that the results “confirm” the first-layer tension should be softened.

The evaluation is limited to one 450M-scale setting and six related multiple-choice benchmarks, with no generative, long-context, robustness, or larger-scale tests. The limitations acknowledge much of this, but it still restricts the contribution’s current reach. Ethical risk is low for the architectural proposal, although inherited web-data bias, memorization/privacy risks, and computational cost are not discussed.

strengths: Originality: ExoFormer is a simple, plausible extension of cross-layer residualization. Moving reusable Q/K/V/gate anchors outside the sequential stack and unifying their normalized mixing across coefficient granularities is a useful architectural idea.

Soundness: The paper evaluates many relevant variants. At roughly 450M parameters, Dynamic ExoFormer improves validation perplexity from 14.64 to 14.09 and average downstream accuracy from 48.80% to 50.27% relative to Gated Attention. The normalization, component, granularity, anchor-depth, and gradient-stability ablations provide useful supporting evidence, while the 1B experiment offers some evidence of scaling.

Significance: The method has modest theoretical FLOP and parameter overhead, and the reported approximately 1.5x token-efficiency improvement could be practically valuable if confirmed under compute-matched evaluation.

Presentation: The architecture and mixing equations are mostly clear, figures and tables are readable, and the appendix provides parameter/FLOP analyses and detailed optimizer and architecture hyperparameters.

The paper is unusually transparent that its current implementation incurs an 8–15% latency overhead despite only about 1.3% theoretical extra FLOPs. Its impact statement also acknowledges possible scaling and misuse concerns; there are no apparent unresolved ethical issues.
weaknesses: The main causal claim—that improvements arise specifically from resolving first-layer tension—is not adequately controlled. ExoFormer adds four full d-by-d anchor matrices (about 4M parameters at the 450M scale), while NuResFormer reuses existing projections. There is no parameter- or compute-matched control that allocates comparable extra capacity without exogenous anchoring. Moreover, the static ExoFormer gains over corresponding NuResFormer variants are only 0.02–0.04 perplexity, and downstream accuracy is mixed: elementwise and scalar improve slightly, whereas headwise decreases. No dynamic NuResFormer counterpart is reported.

All headline results appear to be single runs, with no random-seed repetitions, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly concerning for the 1.47-point average gain across six downstream benchmarks, several of which have small test sets. Figure 2 likewise provides curves without uncertainty, and the 1B result compares only Dynamic ExoFormer against Gated Attention and reports no downstream evaluation.

The Offloading Hypothesis is supported mostly through indirect, post-hoc proxies. High PCA effective rank does not establish preservation of token identity; attention sinks, entropy, and token cosine similarity do not uniquely identify “mix,” “compression,” or “refinement” stages; and refinement onset is assigned from local minima rather than an independently validated criterion. Zeroing a pathway at inference creates a severe distribution shift, so the resulting collapse and the difference between architectures do not by themselves establish specialization or first-layer conflict.

The efficiency claims conflate token efficiency with compute efficiency. The implementation is reported to be 8–15% slower per token, but no compute-matched, wall-clock-matched, energy, memory, or measured-throughput comparison is given. Consequently, claims of environmental benefit and higher throughput—especially for the H1/H2 variants—are not substantiated quantitatively.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the extensive hyperparameter tables. The manuscript does not provide repeated-run seeds, tokenizer and data preprocessing details, the exact FineWeb-Edu validation split, evaluation harness/version and prompts, or checkpoint-selection procedures. The promised code and models are not present in the manuscript. The construction and computational accounting of H1/H2 anchors are also insufficiently specified, and using sequential hidden states as anchor inputs complicates the claimed decoupling.

The empirical scope is narrow for the strength of the conclusions: only 450M and 1B models, one training corpus, one optimizer family, and six mostly commonsense multiple-choice tasks are considered. There are no generation, long-context, robustness, standard language-model benchmark, or optimizer-transfer experiments. The claim that the benefit should be optimizer-agnostic is therefore unsupported.

Some mechanistic explanations are stated too strongly. For example, per-token RMS rescaling does not generally isotropize a representation distribution, and the observed suppression of unnormalized-anchor coefficients is compatible with several explanations besides distributional mismatch. Overall, the architectural result is promising, but the missing controls and uncertainty analysis prevent reliable acceptance of the central claims in the current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: ExoFormer is a concrete, implementable extension of cross-layer residual learning, combining exogenous anchors, normalized mixing across Q/K/V/gates, and static or dynamic coefficients.

Soundness: The empirical study includes useful architectural ablations over coefficient granularity, normalization, anchor depth, and anchor removal, evaluated at approximately 450M parameters with a smaller confirmation at 1B.

Results: Dynamic ExoFormer improves the reported 450M validation perplexity from 14.64 to 14.09 and average downstream accuracy from 48.80 to 50.27 versus gated attention, with only a modest parameter increase. The authors also disclose an important 8–15% measured runtime overhead.

Presentation/reproducibility: The method and major hyperparameters are described clearly, and the appendix provides complexity calculations, training settings, and additional diagnostics. Ethics: The impact statement acknowledges dual-use and scaling uncertainty, and I see no unresolved research-ethics issue that independently prevents publication.
weaknesses: Soundness: No results include multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Many relevant differences are very small—for example, static ExoFormer versus NuResFormer differs by only 0.02–0.04 perplexity—and downstream task scores are noisy enough that the claimed advantages cannot be distinguished reliably from run variance.

The central First-Layer Tension and Offloading claims are not established by the evidence. Gate activations and hidden-state statistics are correlational. Zeroing an extensively used pathway at inference is a severe out-of-distribution intervention, and comparing the resulting collapse between separately trained architectures does not identify first-layer tension. PCA rank and token cosine similarity are also treated as proxies for “token identity” without validation, while task loss under these interventions is not reported.

The study lacks matched controls needed to isolate the source of improvement. ExoFormer adds four privileged projection matrices reused at every layer; there is no equal-parameter or equal-compute widened baseline, alternative input-skip module, or comparable extra-capacity control. Thus the gains cannot confidently be attributed to role decoupling rather than added structured capacity.

Evidence for several components is incomplete. Individual Q, K, V, and gate contributions are not systematically isolated, the claimed divergence of unnormalized Q/K variants is relegated to undocumented preliminary runs, and the benefit of anchor normalization is modest in the reported final metrics. The description of RMSNorm as an “isotropization” operator is questionable because per-token RMS scaling preserves direction and does not itself reduce angular anisotropy.

Significance/generalization: Nearly all comparisons are at 450M parameters on one pretraining corpus; the 1B study appears limited to loss curves for the selected method and one baseline. Evaluation covers six closely related multiple-choice benchmarks, with no generation, long-context, robustness, or broader language-model evaluation. Stronger related architectures discussed in the paper, such as MUDDFormer, Hyper-Connections/mHC, and SkipV1Former, are not experimentally compared.

The headline claim of matching loss with approximately 1.5× fewer tokens is inferred from single training curves without uncertainty or a rigorous scaling analysis. It also obscures the reported 8–15% wall-clock slowdown; the environmental-efficiency claim is unsupported without time, energy, or total-compute measurements.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the stated intention to release code and models: the submission provides no accessible artifact, seeds, tokenizer specification, exact FineWeb-Edu split, evaluation harness/version, or prompts. These omissions are especially consequential given the small reported deltas.

Presentation and limitations: The paper repeatedly presents speculative interpretations as validated causal mechanisms. The limitations discussion mentions extrapolation to 100B+ models but does not adequately acknowledge run variance, missing matched-capacity controls, limited baseline coverage, or the weakness of the identity proxies. Overall, the architecture is promising, but the evidence needs substantial strengthening before others can reliably build on its central conclusions.

strengths: Soundness: The paper evaluates a clear progression of controls—base Transformer, Gated Attention, ResFormer, their naïve combination, normalized internal anchors, and external anchors—and provides useful ablations over Q/K/V/G pathways, normalization, coefficient granularity, dynamic mixing, and anchor depth.

Originality: Learning dedicated exogenous projections for cross-layer attention mixing is a simple but meaningful extension beyond first-layer value reuse. The unified treatment of queries, keys, values, and gate logits is technically interesting and potentially reusable.

Significance: Dynamic ExoFormer improves the 450M model's average six-task accuracy from 48.80 for Gated Attention to 50.27 while reducing validation perplexity from 14.64 to 14.09. The reported 1B learning curves also suggest that the benefit is not confined to one model size.

The normalization results are practically valuable: normalized ExoFormer improves over its unnormalized counterpart (14.13 versus 14.30 perplexity), and the gradient-spike analysis supplies complementary evidence that the normalized architecture trains more stably.

Presentation: The method is clearly formulated, including coefficient granularities, initialization, dynamic modulation, parameter/FLOP overhead, and detailed hyperparameters. Figures and tables are generally legible and the paper distinguishes static, dynamic, internal-anchor, and external-anchor variants well.

Reproducibility and ethics: The paper specifies model dimensions, training tokens, optimizer settings, dataset, sequence length, batch size, precision, evaluation tasks, and theoretical overhead. It also acknowledges measured latency overhead, uncertain scaling beyond 1B parameters, and possible misuse rather than hiding these limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central First-Layer Tension and Offloading Hypothesis is not established as strongly as claimed. Gate profiles and representation statistics are correlational, while zeroing a learned pathway only at inference creates an out-of-distribution intervention. The resulting PCA collapse does not by itself show that token-identity preservation was offloaded or that the first layer faced an optimization conflict.

No repeated runs, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported. This is important because many comparisons are small—for example, static E-ExoFormer versus E-NuResFormer differs by only 0.02 perplexity and 0.17 average accuracy—and individual downstream results fluctuate across tasks.

The external-anchor models have additional parameters (457M versus 453–454M), yet there is no parameter- or compute-matched control that allocates the same capacity to an ordinary Transformer or gated model. Consequently, the experiments do not fully isolate architectural placement from added capacity.

The strongest scaling evidence is limited: the 1B experiment compares only Dynamic ExoFormer with Gated Attention through validation-loss curves, without downstream evaluations or multiple seeds. Generality across datasets, context lengths, optimizers, and substantially larger models therefore remains uncertain.

The claimed 1.5x data efficiency is based on matching validation loss, but the implementation is reported to be 8–15% slower per token. Wall-clock, FLOP-adjusted, and energy-adjusted comparisons are absent, so the practical efficiency and environmental claims are not yet fully supported.

The H1-anchor result complicates the paper's interpretation: an anchor sourced from the first sequential layer is no longer purely external to that stack and may transmit an auxiliary anchor objective back into that layer. The manuscript does not reconcile this with the proposed first-layer tension, despite H1 producing the best perplexity.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete in the manuscript: the exact tokenizer and data preprocessing, evaluation harness and prompts, checkpoint-selection procedure, random seeds, and executable code location are not specified. The statement that code and models will be released cannot substitute for an inspectable artifact during review.

Presentation occasionally overstates the evidence, using terms such as “fundamental,” “confirms,” and “validate” for mechanistic conclusions supported mainly by descriptive metrics. Framing these conclusions as plausible hypotheses would better match the evidence.
